I cried for ten minutes, called my mother, and came out grinning. So that's what I, Sabina, learned that day: tears don't come with labels. Ask, and give people a door.

passage: I'm Yash, and I sit beside Sachin in the planning team. At Friday's meeting our director announced that Mr. Kapur, who'd trained half of us, was "taking early retirement". The director smiled and said it was his choice. I glanced at Sachin. His jaw was clenched, and his eyes were full of tears he wasn't letting fall. I couldn't tell what they meant. Sadness at losing his mentor? Something else? After the meeting he went straight to the stairwell. I waited ten minutes, then took him a cup of tea and stood a little distance away. "Do you want company, or should I leave you be?" He took the tea. "Company's fine." Then, quietly: "It wasn't his choice. They pushed him out. I'm not sad. I'm angry." I nodded. I'd assumed grief. I asked if he wanted to talk to HR about how it was handled, or just let off steam first. "Steam first," he said. "Then HR."

qa.a: Sachin was angry, not only sad, believing Mr. Kapur had been pushed out rather than choosing to leave.

Caught myself doing it again today. Sarika walked in twenty minutes late to the handover, laughing on her phone, and I rolled my eyes so hard my head moved. subtype: Hostile and furious de-escalation [Regulating]
passage:
Saturday night
Worst customer of my life today, and I think I handled it okay.
A woman, Mehak, came into the repair shop shouting that we'd lost her phone. Face red, finger jabbing at me over the counter. Everyone in the shop went silent. My first instinct was to shout back that we don't lose phones. Instead I stayed behind the counter, a good arm's length away, and dropped my voice right down. "I can see you're really upset. Let me look it up with you." She shouted again. I kept my voice slow and low. I didn't say anything like "calm down" or "I'll call security". I just offered a way forward: "If it's not here, the manager will sort a replacement today."
It turned up in the wrong drawer, under another name. When I handed it over, she started crying. Said the photos of her late father were on it.
I told Suresh bhaiya that if she'd come round the counter, I'd have stepped back and called him straight away. Safety first.
Tarun

qa.a: In the wrong drawer, under another name.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling beneath the shouting?
qa.a: Mehak was frightened and grieving, since the phone held photos of her late father, and it came out as fury.

qa.q: How did Tarun de-escalate the situation?
qa.a: Tarun stayed behind the counter at a distance, lowered and slowed the voice, avoided threats, acknowledged her upset and offered a clear way forward.

qa.q: What would have changed if Tarun had shouted back?
qa.a: Mehak's fear and anger would likely have escalated, the shop could have turned into a shouting match, and the phone might not have been found calmly.

Ganga had come about her cancelled ration card, and Damini, the young clerk, was explaining the re-application when Ganga's brother-in-law, Ramkesh, burst in smelling of liquor. "You cancelled it! You people eat the poor!" he shouted, banging the table. Damini stood up slowly and moved so the table stayed between them, near the door. She lowered her voice. "Bhaiya, I hear you. Sit, we'll fill the form together. It can be done today." For a moment he hesitated. Then he picked up the heavy register and raised it. Damini didn't argue. "I'm going to get the sarpanch-ji," she said calmly, and walked straight out of the door. Outside she called the sarpanch and the police helpline. Within minutes the sarpanch and two men from the tea stall arrived and led Ramkesh outside. Ganga, shaking, said, "Madam, I'm sorry." Damini filled in the form with her on the verandah.

passage: Vaibhav, you said Mr. Iyer's long silence in the review means he hates your design. Let me, Joseph, tell you about Mr. Pinto at the shipyard in Kochi. I was twenty-six, presenting my first hull modification. When I finished, Mr. Pinto just sat there, looking at the drawing and tapping his glasses, for maybe a full minute. No words. I'm wondering if we can use it on the other two ships." I'd nearly thrown away my best work because I'd read a pause as a verdict. After that, when a senior went quiet, I'd wait, and then ask, "What are you thinking about it, sir?" Sometimes it was doubt. Often it was interest. The only way to know was to ask. So ask Mr. Iyer.

passage: At the block office in Chhindwara district, the notice came by email at noon: the new primary health centre for Lalit's village had finally been approved. Disha watched Lalit read it. His eyes went wide, he let out a long breath, and when he spoke, his voice was tight and strange. "It's approved." Then he went out onto the verandah and stood very still with his back to everyone. Disha couldn't read it. Was he worried about the land it would take? Upset about something she didn't know? She gave him a few minutes, then went out with two cups of tea and stood beside him. "You looked surprised in there. Are you okay?" He took the tea, eyes wet. "Relieved. My mother had to travel forty kilometres for every check-up last year. Now the village won't have to." Disha nodded and said nothing more, letting him have the quiet. After a while he laughed shakily. "Don't tell anyone I cried at a notice."

qa.q: How far did Lalit's mother have to travel for check-ups?
qa.a: Forty kilometres.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling after reading the notice?
qa.a: Lalit felt surprised and deeply relieved, even tearful, because his mother and village would no longer travel so far for care.

qa.a: She might have offered the wrong comfort or asked awkward questions, missing that he was actually relieved.

grounding: Shows a young professional reading a colleague's widened eyes, sigh and tight voice at news, and a calm check-in revealing relief.

passage: Tushar, you said I look like a statue in meetings. Everyone says it. I'm Gautam, junior auditor, and a blank face is practically part of the job. Last year a client complained to my manager that I seemed "bored and disapproving". My manager didn't guess; she asked me. I explained, and she suggested I add one sentence at the start of meetings: "I keep a neutral face while I work; it doesn't mean anything's wrong." It helped. And then in March my father was in hospital, and my face was the same blank as always, but underneath I was falling apart. The same manager noticed I was coming in earlier and eating nothing. She asked again. I told her. Same face, different meaning. The pattern gave me away, not the face.

subtype: Deadpan and impassive as professional style [Mismatch]
passage: I'm Chinmay, and I sat in on my first disciplinary hearing last month as the note-taker. Usha from HR ran it. For forty minutes, while the employee cried, argued and apologised, Usha's face didn't move. Calm voice, still hands, no nods, no frowns. I honestly couldn't tell whether she believed him, pitied him, or didn't care at all. Afterwards I asked her, carefully, "Do you ever feel anything in those rooms?" She laughed, a bit tiredly. "All the time. If I show it, though, they read my face instead of the facts, and whichever way I lean feels unfair." Then she added, "That one was hard. He reminds me of my brother." I hadn't seen a flicker of that. Over the next weeks I noticed her pattern: impassive in hearings, warm and joking at lunch, and always a walk round the building afterwards. The blankness was a tool, not the whole of her.

qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling during the hearing, as she later said?
qa.a: Usha felt sad and moved, finding the hearing hard because the employee reminded her of her brother, though her face stayed still.

qa.q: What helped Chinmay understand Usha's impassive style?
qa.a: Asking her directly and watching her pattern over weeks: blank in hearings, warm at lunch, a walk afterwards.

qa.a: Chinmay couldn't tell whether she believed the employee, pitied him or didn't care at all.

For three weeks she'd drifted through the staffroom looking flat and tired, answering in a word or two, never joining the tea-time gossip. "Lazy," the PT teacher muttered. "She's lost interest." Yusuf wasn't sure. She still corrected every notebook, and her classes were quiet and orderly. Maybe she was just a private person. Maybe something was wrong. He didn't want to guess or label. One afternoon, when the staffroom emptied, he put a glass of nimbu pani on her desk. "You've looked tired lately. Totally fine if you don't want to say, but is there anything that would help?" She looked up, surprised. "I'm getting over typhoid. The doctor said I could come back, but I'm exhausted by noon." Yusuf nodded. "Want me to take your after-lunch playground duty for a couple of weeks?" "Yes," she said, and her face finally softened.

"But thanks for asking me first. If I ever am, I'll tell you." She put the headphone back on and her face went neutral again, and this time Liam didn't read anything into it.

Tuesday night
Tanvir cried at work today. After the client call where they cancelled his whole project, he went to the pantry, and when I walked in, his eyes were streaming. He turned away fast.
Then Rakesh walked in behind me, saw him, and said, "Arre, be a man, yaar," laughing. Tanvir went red and left.
I kept thinking about it all afternoon. In my family, the men cry at every wedding and funeral and nobody blinks. In Tanvir's, maybe not. Maybe he was ashamed. Maybe he was just furious. I didn't know, and neither did Rakesh.
So at five I messaged him: "Hey, that call sounded brutal. How are you feeling?" He wrote back: "Angry, mostly. Two years of work. The crying just happens when I'm angry, and I hate it." I said I get the same, and that it's nothing to be embarrassed about. He sent back a thumbs-up and "thanks, needed that".
Tomorrow I'm going to say something to Rakesh.
Sharmila
